item.title: Perplexity's Time Machine returns the web as it was on any day in the past year, and the Context API that serves it costs $1 per 1,000 URLs
item.description: A snapshot_as_of parameter on the Search and Context APIs makes retrieval reproducible; with OpenAI's shared ChatGPT-and-Codex meter arriving in December, it is a week for re-reading the usage pages.
item.content:encoded:
A snapshot_as_of parameter on the Search and Context APIs makes retrieval reproducible; with OpenAI's shared ChatGPT-and-Codex meter arriving in December, it is a week for re-reading the usage pages.

Perplexity's November changelog contains a feature that solves one of the quieter problems in building with retrieval: the web moves under your tests. Time Machine adds a snapshot_as_of parameter to the Search API (POST /search) and the Context API (POST /v1/context), and to the Agent API's web_search and fetch_url tools through filters. It takes an RFC 3339 timestamp up to 365 days in the past. Search results come from the copy of each page saved at or before that moment; context fetches are served only from stored copies and are never fetched live; if no copy exists, the response carries a no_content status. The Python library (0.50.0) and TypeScript SDK (0.45.0) accept native datetime objects.

What it costs

Time Machine itself carries no separate price. The Context API, new this month, is billed at $1.00 per 1,000 URLs fetched, with failed fetches free and any criteria scoring billed as Decisions input tokens. The same changelog lists a Monitor API at $0.001 per search run and $0.001 per page run per URL, an Orchestrator API out of private preview, and automatic output-token limits up to 128,000 per generation. Its model price table also confirms third-party rates we track elsewhere: GPT-6.2 Sol at $2 / $0.10 / $10 and Astra at $8 / $0.40 / $40, Gemini 4 Neon at $3 / $0.15 / $15, and Gemini 4 Carbon at $2 / $0.10 / $10 as an introductory rate through November 30, matching the December 1 step-up on our price calendar.

What to build with it

  • Reproducible evals. Fix snapshot_as_of to the date your benchmark was written and the retrieval side stops drifting. Dynamic-benchmark leakage, where a model's search returns a page that discusses the benchmark itself, is contained by date.
  • Temporal honesty tests. Snapshot at T, ask about events after T, and measure whether the model admits it cannot know. This is the cheapest eval of temporal grounding available.
  • Audit trails for agents. An agent that cites a page can now cite the page as of the moment it read it, which is what a compliance reviewer wants.
  • Change detection. Diff the context for a URL across two snapshots to see what a vendor changed in a pricing page or a policy, the job this publication does by hand.

The catch is coverage. A stored copy exists only if Perplexity crawled the page before your timestamp; the no_content rate on niche or fast-changing domains is the number to measure before you commit, and 365 days is a hard floor on how far back you can go.

The other meter

OpenAI confirmed that from December, Plus, Pro and Business subscribers draw ChatGPT conversations and Codex tasks from one shared token-based allowance, with instant chats exempt, usage visible under Settings → Usage, and the options at the cap being to wait, upgrade or buy credits for eligible features. OpenAI has not published the size of the pool and says most users should not see resets more often than today; in late October it reversed a planned halving of Pro 200 limits and doubled allowances on the Pro and Business Premium tiers after a backlash. The practical change is that a developer who runs Codex all afternoon now consumes the same budget the rest of the team uses for chat.

The counter-argument

A metered archive of the web competes with Common Crawl, which is free, irregular and enormous, and with the Internet Archive, which is free and uneven. At $1 per 1,000 URLs, a context-heavy agent that fetches 50 pages a task pays five cents a task before model tokens, which is fine for a research tool and ruinous for a consumer product. And OpenAI's shared meter is, from the vendor's side, a simplification; the complaints will come from the heavy users it was designed to meter.

What to do

  • Measure your no_content rate on a sample of your target URLs at 30, 90 and 300 days back before building on Time Machine.
  • Add snapshot_as_of to every eval harness that touches live search, dated to the day the eval set was frozen.
  • If you run Pro or Business seats with Codex users, pull the Settings → Usage view for your heaviest accounts before December and decide whether they need their own plan.

item.title: Google puts a date on it: AI agents must use Workspace MCP instead of REST from February 1, 2027
item.description: Workspace MCP servers and the CLI went generally available on November 24 with free and paid tiers, the same day Anthropic made MCP Tasks GA and put Skills over MCP into beta.
item.content:encoded:
Workspace MCP servers and the CLI went generally available on November 24 with free and paid tiers, the same day Anthropic made MCP Tasks GA and put Skills over MCP into beta.

November 24 produced two announcements that belong together. Google made its Workspace MCP servers and official Workspace CLI generally available, with standardized usage tiers, new admin policies and an AI Tools Addendum. Anthropic made MCP Tasks and Elicitation generally available in Claude and Claude Code, and put Skills over MCP into public beta. One is the largest data estate in enterprise software declaring a protocol mandatory; the other is the protocol's author adding the pieces that make a server more than a tool list.

What Google actually committed to

MCP servers now cover Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks, with Keep to come, and the CLI targets terminal, virtual machine and container agents. Two tiers: Standard is free with published rate limits, Scaled offers higher quotas, starting with Gmail, Drive and Calendar. Google says over 99% of active developers sit inside Standard. Charging for Scaled begins April 1, 2027, and only for usage above the daily free allowances; projects that neither switch nor get marked internal fall back to Standard limits.

The date that matters more is February 1, 2027, when Google begins technically enforcing that AI agents use MCP rather than calling the REST APIs directly. That is a migration deadline with teeth, announced with roughly fourteen months of notice for billing and ten weeks of notice for enforcement. Google promises at least 90 days' notice for changes and excludes Workspace APIs from Cloud Support's variable fee until at least December 2027.

For administrators, access for external AI tools, MCP servers, the CLI and APIs is managed in one place in the Admin console under Security → API Controls. Admins can set human-in-the-loop confirmation rules and read agent audit logs, agents must identify themselves in OAuth, and existing DLP rules apply without reconfiguration. Granular agent policies are promised "over the coming months" — the gap to watch.

What Anthropic added

Tasks and Elicitation are GA for Pro, Max and Ultra and rolling out to Team and Enterprise. Tasks let a server run work that outlives a single request; Elicitation lets it ask the user for something mid-flight, with Supabase, Railway and GitHub named as adopters. Skills over MCP — a server shipping instructions, not just tools — is in public beta, on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra, needing an admin to enable it on Team plans, with Shopify, HubSpot and Atlassian live and Carta coming. File uploads are listed as rolling out soon. Anthropic puts the ecosystem at over 10,000 connectors for Claude and over 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and says tool search can cut tool-definition context by more than 85% in multi-server setups.

The shape of the bet

Two years after MCP was published, the protocol has moved from a convention between Claude and a handful of servers to the access path a platform vendor will enforce. That is good for anyone who was going to build integrations anyway, and it changes the negotiating position of everyone who was not: the alternative to speaking MCP to Workspace is, from February, no programmatic agent access at all. The free tier covering 99% of developers is the sweetener, and the April 2027 billing date is the part to model.

The caution is that "agents must use MCP" and "MCP is secure" are different claims. A protocol that standardises how a model reaches eight Google apps also standardises the blast radius of a credential, and Skills over MCP means a server can now ship the instructions the model follows, not merely the functions it calls. The last month supplied the counter-examples: router endpoints losing zero-data-retention status, a poisoned package in an agent framework, an agent committing a credential to a public repository.

What to do

Inventory every agent and automation that touches Workspace REST endpoints and give each one an owner and a February deadline. Decide now whether each project is internal — the marking that preserves higher limits inside your subscription — or headed for the Scaled tier, and get the April 2027 cost into next year's budget rather than discovering it. Turn on agent audit logs and set confirmation rules before you need them. On the Anthropic side, if you run Team or Enterprise, decide deliberately whether to enable Skills over MCP, because a server that can ship instructions deserves the same review as a dependency.

What to watch

Whether Google publishes dollar prices for the Scaled tier well before April 2027; what the granular agent policies look like, since today's controls are coarse; whether other suites — Microsoft 365 in particular — set their own MCP deadlines; and whether Skills over MCP reaches Enterprise with admin-level review of what a server's skills contain.

item.title: Anthropic's Claude Ship puts an agent on the whole pull request: PR Steward fixes CI, Approvals can merge-approve, and /ship opens the PR. What engineering leads should configure first
item.description: Code Review was the easy part; the new beta lets an agent act on the findings and, under a policy file you write, approve routine changes without a human, which makes the policy file the most important code in your repo.
item.content:encoded:
Code Review was the easy part; the new beta lets an agent act on the findings and, under a policy file you write, approve routine changes without a human, which makes the policy file the most important code in your repo.

Anthropic on Monday bundled three GitHub-native capabilities into a beta it calls Claude Ship. Code Review, generally available since October 15, reads a pull request and posts findings. PR Steward, new and in beta, acts on them: it fixes failing CI checks, resolves merge conflicts, responds to reviewer comments, and after every push leaves a comment explaining what changed and how to roll it back. Claude Approvals, also beta, applies an approval policy written in plain language and stored in the repository, and can approve routine changes or escalate them to named humans. A new /ship command in the Claude Code CLI and desktop app chains the lot: push, open the PR, review, iterate until checks pass.

Availability is Claude Team and Enterprise on GitHub repositories only. Organisations with zero-data-retention, HIPAA or customer-managed-key configurations are excluded for now. Review and Steward are billed on token usage under admin-set monthly limits; /ship counts toward normal Claude Code usage. Eligible Enterprise customers can claim at least $10,000 of Claude Ship credits until January 15, 2027.

The boundaries Anthropic drew

PR Steward cannot approve or merge. Claude Approvals can approve, but only within the policy file, which takes effect once it is on the default branch, and GitHub branch protection still applies on top. Anthropic recommends starting in observe-only mode on a single repository with a spend limit, and says the policy can take Code Review findings and custom classifiers as inputs. A developer steers the agent with @claude in PR comments and stops it with @claude stop. Anthropic's internal evidence is that merged pull requests on the Claude Code team more than doubled from June to September while the share of reverted PRs fell by more than 40%; the company quotes itself, so treat it as a vendor claim.

Why the policy file is the real product

This is the first mainstream release in which an agent's output can satisfy a required review on a protected branch. In GitHub's model, a required approval is a security control; CODEOWNERS and branch protection exist to keep a single compromised account from shipping code alone. A natural-language policy that auto-approves, say, dependency bumps and documentation changes is reasonable. The same file with a loosely worded clause is a path from a prompt injection in a PR description to an approved merge. The site's security coverage of the last fortnight, the Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI poisoning and the Together AI credential leak, both started with an agent doing something plausible inside a repository.

The counter-argument

Teams already run auto-merge for Dependabot and have for years; the novelty is scope, not kind. And the alternative to agent approval is review queues that stretch for days while agents write most of the code, which is the situation Anthropic says it was in. The question is not whether to allow it but what is routine enough to allow.

What to do

Enable Code Review only for the first two weeks and measure how many findings reviewers act on. Add PR Steward on one repository with a monthly cap and watch the rollback comments; they are the audit trail. Before you turn on Approvals, put the policy file under CODEOWNERS, require two human reviews for changes to it, keep the GitHub rule that a human approval is still required on anything touching auth, payments or infrastructure, and run observe-only mode until you can list what the agent would have approved and agree with every line. Then expand by file path, not by repository.

item.title: Inkling 2 Mini: a 26.4B open-weight model that runs its middle layers three times, fits in 20 GB and scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified. What developers get, what it costs on Tinker, and where it falls short
item.description: Thinking Machines' smallest model is the first mainstream release built around looping rather than depth, and it lands on a Mac with 32 GB of memory under an Apache 2.0 licence.
item.content:encoded:
Thinking Machines' smallest model is the first mainstream release built around looping rather than depth, and it lands on a Mac with 32 GB of memory under an Apache 2.0 licence.

Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini on Friday, the third and smallest member of its Inkling 2 family and the first that most developers can run on the machine in front of them. The weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0, with day-one support in Ollama for Macs with at least 32 GB of memory, on Nvidia's DGX Spark, and in SGLang, vLLM, llama.cpp and Unsloth GGUF builds. The checkpoint is about 20 GB.

The architecture

The headline number is 26.4 billion total parameters with 3.4 billion active per token, but the interesting figure is 48. The model stores 24 layers in four blocks of six. The first and last blocks run once per token; the two middle blocks run three times, so each token passes through 48 layer applications while the memory footprint is that of 24. Counting the loops, the company gives 5.4 billion weight activations per token and uses that figure in its comparison tables. Training started with 8 of 384 experts active per layer, pruned to 128 experts per layer partway through, then ran about a trillion tokens of distillation and reinforcement learning over 2.2 trillion tokens. Twenty of the 24 layers are stored natively in NVFP4, the remaining four in MXFP8, which is why the file is so small. A research variant with a variable number of loops ships alongside it.

The numbers

Thinking Machines claims the best open-weight results under 100 billion total parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 at 48.2% and the Vals Index at 46.5%. It reports 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified, 77.9% on the hard split of SWE-bench Pro v2, 71.6% on Terminal Bench 2.1 against 73.0% for Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B, 79.0% on BrowseComp, 82.7% on MCP Atlas, and 84.5% and 49.3% on ARC-AGI versions 1 and 2. On the Artificial Analysis index it scores 20.1, tied with Qwen3.8-27B. The company is candid about the weaknesses: 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints, both tests of following long multi-turn or heavily constrained instructions, which is exactly where a looped small model would be expected to struggle. The blog does not publish a head-to-head table against Inkling 2 Small; it says Mini approaches Small on a hard GPU-programming set and on a controllability measure.

Two caveats for anyone reading these as purchasing data. All figures are self-reported and the agentic ones depend on scaffolding. And the model card lists a 32 GB hardware floor even though the checkpoint is 20 GB, because activations and the KV cache for its 1 million token context need room.

What it costs

There is no serverless inference price for Mini yet; Thinking Machines' serverless tier still lists Inkling 2 Small at $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.00 output with a 256K context. On the Tinker training platform, Mini is priced at $0.15 per million prefill tokens, $0.015 cached, $0.50 per million sampled tokens, and $0.75 or $1.50 per million training tokens depending on whether you use the 64K or 256K context option. We have added those rates to the pricing tracker with a note that they are Tinker sampling rates rather than an API list price.

What to do

If you run coding agents on developer laptops or inside a VPC, this is the model to benchmark this week against Qwen3.8-27B and IBM's Granite 4.1 on your own tasks, with attention to how it handles long conversations and multi-step instructions. If you fine-tune, the Tinker route gives you a looped architecture without writing a training loop. And if you ship it, read the Apache 2.0 notice obligations once; they are light, but they exist, and the open-source licences explainer on this site covers the differences from the Llama-style licences you may be used to.

item.title: Perplexity's Brain: an agent memory that records its own work and rewrites its skills overnight, with correctness up 25% on repeat tasks. What to copy, and what to guard
item.description: Memory about the user is old news; memory about what the agent did, what failed and what was corrected is the new layer, and it is also a new place for bad instructions to persist.
item.content:encoded:
Memory about the user is old news; memory about what the agent did, what failed and what was corrected is the new layer, and it is also a new place for bad instructions to persist.

Perplexity has added a memory layer called Brain to its Computer agent, available as a research preview to Max and Enterprise Max subscribers. The design inverts the usual meaning of agent memory. Rather than storing facts about the user, their preferences, contacts and projects, Brain stores a record of the work itself: what the agent did on each task, what succeeded, what failed and what the user corrected. It builds that record into a context graph, reviews it at set intervals, typically overnight, and uses the review to update the skills and context the agent loads the next time it runs. The updated material lives in what Perplexity calls an LLM wiki, loaded automatically into the agent's sandbox and revised incrementally, and every entry links back to the session, file or source it was derived from.

The numbers

Perplexity reports early measurements rather than a benchmark: answer correctness up 25% on tasks the agent has encountered before, recall up 16%, and the cost of tasks that need historical context down 13%, because the agent no longer re-derives what it already learned. All three are internal figures with no published test set, and all three are scoped to repeated work. Nothing is claimed for tasks the agent has never seen, which is the honest boundary of the approach: a memory of past work helps when the future resembles the past.

Why it matters

Agent skills, the reusable instruction files that tell a model how to carry out a class of task, have become the main way teams encode process knowledge, and they are maintained by hand. Someone notices the agent keeps mishandling an expense-report format, edits the skill, and hopes the edit generalises. Brain automates that loop and, importantly, keeps the provenance of each change. That second part is what separates a usable system from a black box: when the agent's behaviour shifts, a reviewer can trace the new rule back to the session that produced it. The economics follow. If a meaningful share of enterprise agent work is repetitive, a 13% cost reduction on context-heavy tasks compounds across a workforce of agents, and the correctness gain reduces the human review that currently dominates the real cost of agent deployments.

The risk

A self-editing instruction layer is also a self-persisting attack surface. Indirect prompt injection today has to succeed in the session where the poisoned document is read. With an overnight review that converts observed sessions into standing skills, a malicious instruction encountered on Monday can become part of the agent's default behaviour on Tuesday, and it will carry a plausible provenance link because it did come from a real session. Perplexity's traceability helps detection; it does not prevent the write. The second risk is quieter: an agent that optimises for last week's tasks can drift away from the general behaviour the vendor shipped, and the drift is invisible unless you evaluate on held-out tasks. Google's GTIG report this week described a backdoor delivered through an agent's settings file; a memory layer is a richer version of the same target.

What to do

If you build agents, copy the architecture, not the claim: a work log with provenance, a scheduled review that proposes skill edits, and a human or policy gate between proposal and load. Keep memory entries in version control and diff them, treat the review job's output as untrusted input, and ban it from writing anything that grants permissions or changes tool access. If you buy agents, ask vendors three questions: can I see and approve what the agent learned overnight, can I roll a memory back, and are gains measured on tasks the agent has not seen. If you are a security team, add agent memory stores to the list of places you look for persistence; the CISO agent checklist on this site has a control for configuration files, and memory is the same control.

What to watch

Whether Perplexity publishes an evaluation with a held-out set, whether memory entries get a signing or approval step before they load, and how quickly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google ship equivalents; all three have skills systems and none has yet described one that rewrites them unattended.

item.title: MAI Code 2 lands in GitHub Copilot: Microsoft says 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5%. What the claims hide, and what Ignite changed for anyone building agents
item.description: Microsoft now ships its own frontier-adjacent coding model inside the subscription it already sells, and starts metering agent run-time in Foundry on December 1. The benchmark averages are the least important part.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft now ships its own frontier-adjacent coding model inside the subscription it already sells, and starts metering agent run-time in Foundry on December 1. The benchmark averages are the least important part.

Microsoft AI released MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash on Tuesday as Ignite opened in San Francisco. Both are generally available in GitHub Copilot the same day: Code 2 on the Pro, Pro+, Max, Business and Enterprise plans, Flash additionally on Free and Student, across VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse, the command line, the cloud coding agent and the mobile app. Flash is also in limited preview on Microsoft Foundry, and both are promised soon on OpenRouter, Vercel, OpenCode and Kilo.

The claims

Microsoft's numbers are relative, not absolute. It says Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of its cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of its cost, averaged across DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1. Flash is described as comparable to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of their prices. A blind front-end preference test of 258 annotators preferred Code 2 to GPT-6 Sol 67% of the time on the model page and 64% on the Ignite page. No raw benchmark scores are published, no per-token price is published, and the cost ratios are computed on a 50% promotional price with no end date. A reader cannot reconstruct any of the comparisons from the announcement.

That does not make the model bad. It makes the announcement a marketing document, and the right response is to put Code 2 on your own repository with your own task set and measure completion rate per dollar against whatever you use now.

What else Ignite shipped

MAI Cyber 2 Flash is available to defenders through the Microsoft Defender programme and scored 83.2% on CyberGym end-to-end in a third-party test. MAI Image 2.7 Flash is priced at about $10 per thousand images and MAI Realtime 1 from one cent per audio minute. Decision 1.1 is generally available with a claimed 4,000 customers and a claim of being 50 times faster and 79 times cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol on the scoring tasks it is built for. GPT-6.2 is described as coming to Foundry. The Copilot harness, Microsoft's agent runtime, enters public preview in Foundry Agent Service with more than twenty frontier models behind it, and runtime billing begins on December 1. GitHub's changelog of November 16 also retired Claude Opus 4.8, Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Terra from the Copilot picker, added Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon, and introduced an Agents inbox in VS Code.

Why it matters more than a benchmark

Microsoft pays OpenAI for every Copilot completion served by an OpenAI model. A first-party model that it judges good enough for 98% of the work at 40% of the cost is a direct improvement in Copilot's gross margin and a reduction in what flows to OpenAI, on the same week OpenAI cut its own flagship price. It also changes the question a Copilot buyer should ask. Until now the pitch was access to the best models from every lab. From today the default may be Microsoft's own, and the routing decision is made in Redmond.

The counter-argument

Averages across four benchmarks hide the distribution; a model that is 98% as good on average can be 80% as good on the long-horizon tasks that matter most and 110% on the easy ones. Microsoft's own blind test used front-end tasks, the category where current models are strongest. And the deprecation list shows the cost of building on a picker: three models that teams had tuned prompts for disappeared on a Sunday.

What to do

Run Code 2 and Flash through your evaluation set this week and record cost per merged change, not per token. Set your Copilot organisation policy explicitly rather than inheriting the new default. If you use the Foundry harness preview, estimate December's bill now from the metering documentation. And treat the model-picker deprecations as a recurring event: keep prompts and evals portable across models, because the next retirement will also arrive on a weekend.

item.title: macOS 27.3 tightens Full Disk Access because of AI agents: silent denials, no one-click toggle, and a 'Private Folders' permission in the code. What agent developers should do before December
item.description: Apple is removing the shortcut that let an assistant app earn blanket access to Mail, Messages and backups with a single switch, and the scoped alternative is not ready; onboarding flows that depend on the old path break next month.
item.content:encoded:
Apple is removing the shortcut that let an assistant app earn blanket access to Mail, Messages and backups with a single switch, and the scoped alternative is not ready; onboarding flows that depend on the old path break next month.

Apple's macOS 27.3 has been in developer beta since November 2 and is expected to ship in December. Its most consequential change for anyone building an AI assistant on the Mac is not a feature but a removal: the shortcut that let an app obtain Full Disk Access with a single switch is going away, and Apple has said in as many words that AI agents are the reason.

What Full Disk Access is and what changes

Full Disk Access is the permission that unlocks the parts of macOS the sandbox normally hides: the Mail and Messages databases, Safari data, Time Machine backups and some administrative settings. Until now, when an app tried to read a protected file without the permission, macOS denied the request and added the app to the Full Disk Access list in System Settings, so a user could enable it with one toggle. Installers for assistant apps have leaned on that path: try to read the iMessage database, fail, tell the user to flip the switch.

Code in the 27.3 beta, examined and published by the developer known as pdfu on November 7, shows the attempt is still denied and is logged, but the app is no longer added to the list. The user has to open System Settings, Privacy and Security, Full Disk Access, and add the app by hand, by dragging it in or using the plus button. Apple's October 2 developer post set the principle: users who want to grant this level of access "can only do so with very explicit user action," because "the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially" as agents become more capable and autonomous.

The same code references a "Private Folders" permission that would grant access folder by folder or database by database, the obvious answer to the assistant that only wants your messages. It is not functional in the current beta and Apple has not confirmed it will ship. Monday's beta 2 is reported to add warnings and controls over what AI automation apps can see and do; Apple has published no release notes describing them, so treat the specifics as unconfirmed until it does.

Why Apple is doing this

The demand driving Full Disk Access requests is iMessage. Assistants that read your texts can draft replies, summarise threads and schedule from them, and there is no narrower permission that gets them there, so they ask for everything. 9to5Mac's Michael Burkhardt makes the fair criticism that removing the toggle does not solve that: a user who wants the feature will still grant blanket access, with more friction and the same exposure. The scoped permission is the real fix, and it is the part that is not ready.

Apple's calculation is visible in the sequencing. Make blanket access harder first, so the number of apps holding it stops growing; ship the scoped permission when it works; then, presumably, tighten further. The Mac is also the machine where third-party agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and the coding-tool vendors run with the most autonomy, which makes it the right place to draw the line before the pattern spreads to iOS.

What to do

If you ship a Mac agent, test onboarding on 27.3 beta today. Replace "flip the toggle" instructions with a guided drag-into-Settings flow and screenshots, and expect conversion to fall. Separate features that need Messages or Mail from those that do not, so a user who declines blanket access still gets a working product. Design your data model around folder-scoped access now, because when Private Folders ships, the apps that ask for one database will be the ones Apple features and the ones that ask for everything will be the ones it warns about. If you run a fleet of Macs, add the new denial log to your endpoint monitoring: an agent that probes protected paths it was never granted is telling you something. And whichever platform you build for, read Apple's wording as the industry's next default: an assistant gets what the user explicitly hands over, nothing more.

item.title: llama.cpp 1.0.0 after 3.5 years: semantic versioning, 35 deprecated functions gone, FP8 KV cache. What the stability promise changes for local AI
item.description: The engine under Ollama, LM Studio and most on-device inference now promises that breaking changes arrive only with a major version; for the teams that link libllama, that is the end of a fortnightly maintenance tax.
item.content:encoded:
The engine under Ollama, LM Studio and most on-device inference now promises that breaking changes arrive only with a major version; for the teams that link libllama, that is the end of a fortnightly maintenance tax.

On Thursday Georgi Gerganov's ggml-org released llama.cpp 1.0.0 and ggml 1.0.0, three and a half years after the project began as a weekend port of Meta's first Llama weights to a MacBook. The headline is not a feature. It is a promise: from now on, libllama and libggml follow semantic versioning. A major version means a breaking change to the public C API or ABI. A minor version adds backends, model architectures or new API without breaking old callers. A patch fixes bugs and changes nothing else. An official llama.cpp release is only tagged when its bundled ggml matches a released ggml, so system-wide installs from Debian or Homebrew stay consistent.

Why that matters more than it sounds

llama.cpp is the inference engine beneath a large share of local and on-device AI: Ollama, LM Studio, Jan and dozens of apps link it or shell out to it, and the GGUF format it introduced is how quantised open-weight models are distributed. Until now the project shipped a numbered build almost daily and reserved the right to change its API at any time. Teams that depended on it either froze a commit and fell behind on model support, or tracked the head and absorbed breakage. The release post acknowledges this directly, noting that many downstream applications depend on the work and that the maintainers will prioritise code quality and architectural control.

What is in 1.0.0

The deprecated public API is removed, 35 functions in all, so anything still calling them must migrate. The NextN speculative-decoding API moves from an extension header into the public llama.h. Memory handling gains FP8 KV caches and a host-memory cache for mixture-of-experts models with a configurable CPU share, which is the feature that lets a sparse model larger than video memory run by keeping cold experts in system RAM. New model support includes Kimi K3.1 Pro and vision for Kimi K3.1, a text-to-speech model and several text architectures, taking the supported count past 150 variants. The server fixes server-side request forgery, CORS and DNS-rebinding issues, restricts the HF_TOKEN to huggingface.co hosts, and adds an OpenAI-compatible speech endpoint. Pre-built packages cover Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and iOS through Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget and an XCFramework. Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel supply self-hosted CI runners; Hugging Face infrastructure handles the rest.

The counter-argument

A version number is a developer commitment, not a code freeze. The release post is explicit that change continues; what changes is the signalling. End users of Ollama or LM Studio will notice nothing on Friday. And semantic versioning cuts both ways: a project that has moved fast for three years may find that the next genuinely necessary API break now requires a 2.0 and a migration guide, which is friction the daily-build era never had. Whether the maintainers hold the line through the next wave of architectures, this week alone brought a 594B NVFP4 model and a 1.6T MoE, is the test.

What to do

If you ship software that links libllama: move to the 1.0.0 tag, run your test suite against the removed deprecated functions, and set your dependency to 1.x with minor-version updates allowed. If you distribute GGUF models: nothing changes in the format, but check that your quantisation recipes still load. If you are evaluating on-device or on-premises inference for a product: the FP8 KV cache and MoE host cache are worth benchmarking against your current serving stack on the models you actually run, with attention to quality at long context, not only tokens per second. If you are an executive weighing self-hosting: the runtime's stability was the argument against; the GPU bill and the serving-stack gaps we described for Inkling 2 Small on Thursday are the arguments that remain.

item.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: $1.50 / $7.50 flat across a 1M context, 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash, and the end of the Flash brand
item.description: Google's new 'daily driver' for agents costs double its promotional predecessor but removes the long-context surcharge and reports a 57% Terminal-Bench score against Flash's 18%.
item.content:encoded:
Google's new 'daily driver' for agents costs double its promotional predecessor but removes the long-context surcharge and reports a 57% Terminal-Bench score against Flash's 18%.

Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12 and described it as the model it wants developers to run agents on by default. It is priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across a 1 million-token context, with up to 1 million output tokens. The post does not list a cached-input price or any promotional period, which is a change from the Carbon and Argon launches, both of which carry introductory rates that end on November 30.

What it replaces

Hydrogen is presented as the upgrade path for teams on Gemini 3.8 Flash, and the Flash name does not appear in the new line-up: Hydrogen is the fast execution model, Carbon and Argon do the deep reasoning. In Google's Orchestrator setup, Carbon plans and Hydrogen acts as a worker or verifier; Google says that combination reached near-Carbon task success on Terminal-Bench 4.0 using about 24% less quota and finishing about 19% faster.

The headline numbers are Google's own. Hydrogen scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (Argon is 50) and 54 at the new xhigh level. On Terminal-Bench 4.1 it reports 57% against 18.2% for 3.8 Flash. It claims the top spot on Vals' Tax Agent Bench (52.3%) and a tie for first on Legal Research Bench (55.8%), 58.8% on HLE-Diamond and 71.6% on Agents' Last Exam. Early partners saw 2x to 2.8x faster runs with 12% to 23% fewer tokens on SQL and graph workloads. One image caption in the post compares against "3.5 Flash" while the text says 3.8; treat the Flash comparison as approximate until independent numbers appear.

The price, properly compared

On the face of it Hydrogen is twice the price of 3.8 Flash. But Flash's $0.75 / $3.75 is a promotional rate that ends on December 31 and returns to $1.50 / $7.50 on January 1, 2027. From that date the two models cost the same per token, and Hydrogen's claimed token efficiency becomes the whole cost argument. The flat long-context price also matters more than it looks: Google's Pro tiers historically charge more above 200K tokens, and OpenAI's GPT-6 line doubles input above 272K. An agent that keeps a large repository or document set in context pays no surcharge here.

Against the field, Hydrogen sits between OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra ($1 / $5) and GPT-6.1 Sol ($2 / $10), and 25% below Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10). It undercuts Carbon's post-promo $4 / $20 by more than half.

Safety and reliability claims

Google leans hard on agent behaviour: an 81% reduction in over-reach on agentic tasks, 12x fewer misaligned actions and task shortcuts across tool-use evals, a 96.7% score on an internal agent honesty test, and a 2.3x improvement on Gray Swan's indirect prompt-injection benchmark. Fabricated claims are said to be down more than 5x versus Flash. These are internal evaluations; the IPI figure is the one worth asking Google to document, because it is the number a security team will be asked about.

What to test

Run your existing Flash eval set at Hydrogen's high thinking level and record tokens per task, not just accuracy, since the token-efficiency claim is where the savings live. Test a long-context case above 272K tokens to see the flat price in your own bill. If you use Antigravity or Gemini Enterprise, try the Carbon-plans, Hydrogen-executes split before buying Carbon seats for every workflow. And budget for Flash's January step-up either way: Hydrogen's launch is the clearest sign yet that the promotional era for Google's mid-tier is closing.

item.title: Gemini Decision 1: 1,000 questions per call, 150 ms, $0.10 per million input tokens and no output bill
item.description: Google and OpenAI now both sell decisions as a product separate from text; here is what the new API does, where it beats a Flash model, and the three places in an agent loop to try it first.
item.content:encoded:
Google and OpenAI now both sell decisions as a product separate from text; here is what the new API does, where it beats a Flash model, and the three places in an agent loop to try it first.

Google launched the Gemini Decisions API on November 11. The model behind it, gemini-decision-1, does not write anything. It takes a shared input of up to 256,000 tokens, in text, images, audio, video or PDF, and up to 1,000 independent questions about that input, then scores each question's options in a single forward pass and returns probabilities and confidence scores. Questions can be yes/no checks, multiple choice with between 2 and 255 options, or rubric scores.

The numbers

Google quotes 150 to 250 milliseconds end to end, with median model compute of 50 to 100 milliseconds, and says performance barely changes between one and 100 questions per request. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charge; shared input is billed once per request, while each question adds its own instruction and criteria tokens. Google says the model is nearly five times cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite across its shared benchmark suite and claims the lowest calibration error against competing systems on agent routing, reasoning, ranking and multimodal tasks. It is live in Google AI Studio with a free tier, and integrations are rolling out through OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM and Pydantic AI. Context caching and the Batch API are not supported. All figures are Google's own.

Why a model that cannot talk

Most of the calls inside a production agent are not generation. They are decisions: which tool to call, which model tier to route to, whether a response violates a policy, which of five retrieved chunks matters, what score a draft deserves. Teams have been making those calls by asking a small generative model to answer in one word, then parsing the word, then retrying when the model adds a sentence. A scoring head removes the parsing, returns a probability instead of a token, and runs in a fraction of the time because there is no decode loop. Google says it uses the model to route Gemini Notebook queries between tiers and reasoning levels, cutting latency for everyday queries by up to 40%, to pick emoji reactions from more than 200 options in its CC assistant, and as a safety layer in Search that flags adversarial behaviour involving MCP tools. That last one is the most interesting: a cheap judge that cannot generate text is a sound thing to put in front of agents that can.

The competition

OpenAI launched its own Decisions API in October on GPT-6 Luna, with up to 400 questions per request, the same $0.10 per million starting price and a claim of up to ten times the speed of its Responses API. TypeSafe's Jev sells a similar product. Google's edge on paper is question count, 256K multimodal context and the free tier; OpenAI's is a head start of a month and the Luna model's wider availability. Both vendors chose the same price, which tells you the market has already settled on what a decision should cost.

The counter-argument

A decision model is only as good as the options you give it, and it cannot tell you when none of them fit. Open-ended problems, anything that needs an explanation a human will read, and tasks where the error mode is 'the question was wrong' still need generation. The calibration claim is Google's, measured on Google's suite; routing decisions that look confident but are not are worse than slow ones. And lock-in cuts the other way: a pipeline built around 1,000 questions per call does not port cleanly to a 400-question API.

What to build with it first

Start with the three calls in your agent loop that already return one word: model routing, tool selection and the pass/fail policy check before a response goes out. Log the existing Flash answer and the Decision 1 probability side by side for a week and measure agreement, latency and cost. Then try batch grading of evals, where the no-output-charge pricing matters most. Keep a generative fallback for anything the model scores below a threshold you set from your own data, not Google's. And register the model in your pricing tracker as a separate line, because your bill is about to split into generation, retrieval and decisions.

item.title: AlphaProof Code verified Signal's protocol code with 6.5 million lines of Lean in four weeks: what AI-written proofs mean for the software you depend on
item.description: DeepMind's five-person team used agents on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to prove security properties of libsignal at the machine-code level; the trusted part is the 26,000 lines of spec, and that is where review now belongs.
item.content:encoded:
DeepMind's five-person team used agents on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to prove security properties of libsignal at the machine-code level; the trusted part is the 26,000 lines of spec, and that is where review now belongs.

Google DeepMind published AlphaProof Code on November 10, a system in which human experts and AI agents together produce machine-checked proofs that software meets a formal specification. Its first target was libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal protocol that also underpins encryption in WhatsApp and Google Messages. The team proved forward secrecy, post-compromise security and authentication for the post-quantum PQXDH handshake and the Triple Ratchet, for libsignal version 0.105.4 and the spqr library at 1.6.0, and it proved them about the compiled AArch64 machine code rather than the protocol design.

How it worked

Five researchers spent four weeks. Humans and agents running on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the specifications, the statements of what had to be true, and the semantics of the instructions and system calls involved: about 26,000 lines in total, covering 467 instructions and 31 system calls. Agents on Carbon then generated roughly 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs. Lean, the proof assistant, rejects any proof that does not follow, so the volume of generated text is checked mechanically rather than read. To show the method catches real flaws, the team re-inserted two historical, already-patched libsignal bugs and demonstrated that the security theorems fail on each build. The specifications and proofs are being released under Apache 2.0 in a public repository; a full rebuild reportedly needs between 15 and 34 GiB of memory.

For comparison, the seL4 microkernel's verification took about twenty person-years and CompCert's verified compiler about six. Signal's chief technology officer, Ehren Kret, said the work gives Signal greater confidence in its code's privacy guarantees.

What it does not cover

DeepMind is specific about the limits. The proofs apply to its own build of libsignal, run through a small command-line wrapper, not to the Signal, WhatsApp or Google Messages applications. Side channels, such as timing, are out of scope for parts of the analysis. Trust-on-first-use behaviour was not exercised. There is no quantum security guarantee, only the classical properties, and the proofs carry a vacuity bound after roughly 25,000 messages in a session. None of those is a flaw in the result; each is a reminder that a proof is only as broad as its statement.

Why this matters for developers

Formal verification has been the gold standard for safety-critical code and almost nobody has used it, because the specification and proof effort cost more than the software. If agents can do the proof-writing at this scale, the cost moves to the specification: deciding, precisely, what the code must guarantee. That is a smaller job, but it is the one that requires judgment, and it is where errors become invisible. A proof that your code satisfies the wrong spec is worth nothing, and Lean cannot tell you the spec is wrong. The practical change is that review effort for critical libraries should move from reading implementations to reading and arguing about specifications, and that "is there a machine-checked spec for this" becomes a reasonable question to ask a vendor.

It also matters that the agents ran on two vendors' models. Google reported the result on the day it opened Gemini 4 Carbon to all paying developers, and the Carbon-for-cyber variant leads Google's patching benchmark; the implication is that proof generation is a product category, not a one-off.

The counter-argument

This is a Google research result announced alongside a Google model launch, using a target that Signal cooperated on. Nobody outside DeepMind has yet rebuilt the proofs. Proof volume is not a measure of assurance; 6.5 million lines says the agents were prolific, not that the 26,000-line spec is right, and the two re-injected bugs were chosen by the team. Four weeks also followed years of groundwork in Lean, in instruction semantics and in prior verification research that the announcement compresses. The honest claim is narrower: for a well-understood protocol with a cooperative maintainer, AI reduced the proof effort by one to two orders of magnitude.

What to do

If you ship or depend on cryptographic libraries, read the released specification rather than the headline, and compare it with the properties your threat model actually needs. If you maintain a critical open-source library, consider publishing a formal statement of its guarantees now; the proof may follow sooner than you expect, and the spec is the part that needs your knowledge. For security teams, add verified-build status to the questions you ask of messaging, VPN and key-management vendors, and treat machine-code-level proofs as the standard to ask for, since design-level proofs leave the compiler and build pipeline out. And watch for reproductions: the repository is public, and the first independent rebuild will say more than the announcement.

item.title: Muse Ember at $0.10 and LongCat-2.5 under MIT: the budget tier is now where agent costs are decided
item.description: Meta's smallest model matches Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis index at a third of the cost per task, and Meituan has handed developers a 1.6-trillion-parameter model to run themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Meta's smallest model matches Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis index at a third of the cost per task, and Meituan has handed developers a 1.6-trillion-parameter model to run themselves.

Two releases this week moved the cheap end of the model market, which is where most agent tokens are actually spent. Meta launched Muse Ember, its smallest multimodal model, and Meituan published the full weights of LongCat-2.5 under the MIT licence.

Muse Ember

Ember is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 for cached input and $0.50 for output on prompts up to 200K tokens; above that, all three rates triple. It takes text, image, audio and video input, has a 1-million-token window, and is positioned explicitly for repeated agent sub-tasks: tool calls, routing, extraction, document summarisation and coding sub-steps. It is available through Meta's own model API and on Google Cloud Marketplace.

The list price matches Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna exactly. What differs is behaviour. Artificial Analysis, which tests models independently, scores Ember 36 on its Intelligence Index, level with Haiku 5.5, but measures its cost per task at $0.14 against Haiku's $0.41, because Ember emits roughly a third as many output tokens to reach the same answers. On the Coding Agent Index inside Meta's Muse Code harness it scores 46 against 37 for Claude Code with Haiku and 31 for Codex with GPT-6 Luna. Its weaknesses are also measurable: 27.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 against Haiku's 34.9%, and 21.1% accuracy on the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, where it declines to answer 64% of questions. For a model meant to sit inside a loop rather than talk to a user, declining is often the right behaviour.

LongCat-2.5

Meituan, the Chinese delivery company that has quietly become a serious model lab, released the LongCat-2.5 checkpoint on Hugging Face on November 9, a week after announcing the model. It is a mixture-of-experts design with about 1.6 trillion total parameters and roughly 48 billion active per token, with vision input, a hosted API at a limited-time $0.30 / $1.20, and serving optimisations including 4-bit expert weights on Chinese accelerators. Meituan's own figures put it at 88.4 on Terminal Bench v2.1, within a point of GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5, and 64.6 on DeepSWE v1.1, up from 9.7 for LongCat-2.0.

The caveats are the usual ones for vendor tables: the closed baselines Meituan chose are a generation old, Terminal Bench v4.0 leaderboard scores for GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 are far higher, and a 1.6T checkpoint is not something most teams will self-host. The licence is the news. MIT terms impose no usage restrictions, and unlike DeepSeek, which a Department of Homeland Security order excluded from federal civilian procurement in October, no US restriction currently names Meituan.

The counter-argument

Cheap tokens invite waste. A budget model that is three times cheaper per task but is called ten times more often inside a poorly designed agent loop costs more, not less, and Ember's 3x surcharge above 200K tokens punishes exactly the long-context agent patterns Meta is marketing it for. Open weights also shift cost rather than removing it: hosting LongCat-2.5 well needs multi-GPU nodes and operations skill that a $0.30 API rate makes hard to justify.

What to do

Instrument your agents to report cost per completed task, not tokens. Move the mechanical steps, routing, extraction, tool-call formatting and summarisation, to Ember or Haiku and keep the planning step on a mid-tier model. Cap context before the 200K cliff. If you are evaluating LongCat-2.5, test it through a hosted provider first and only consider self-hosting once you know the workload is stable. And re-read your vendor concentration policy: three different companies now anchor the three price tiers in our tracker.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol discount ends November 30. Here is the price ladder to move to
item.description: Two vendors' promotional rates expire within a day of each other. OpenAI's pricing page now shows four GPT-6 tiers from $0.10 to $10 per million tokens, and our tracker has caught up.
item.content:encoded:
Two vendors' promotional rates expire within a day of each other. OpenAI's pricing page now shows four GPT-6 tiers from $0.10 to $10 per million tokens, and our tracker has caught up.

OpenAI's API pricing page now carries a footnote developers should read before the end of the month: promotional pricing for GPT-5.6 Sol is available until November 30, 2026. Since August 21 the model has been billed at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output, a cut from its $5 / $30 list rate that OpenAI announced as a three-month promotion. On December 1 the list rate returns, a 25% increase on input and 50% on output for anyone still on the model.

It lands a day after Google's launch pricing on Gemini 4 Argon ends, taking that model from $2 / $10 to $4 / $20. Two of the three largest API vendors are re-pricing within 24 hours of each other, which is a good moment to look at the whole ladder.

The ladder OpenAI actually wants you on

Our pricing tracker had been carrying GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna from secondary sources. Reading OpenAI's model pages directly today, we confirmed those rows and found four GPT-6-generation tiers that were not in the tracker at all. All carry a 1.05-million-token context window and 128K maximum output, and all double input rates and add 50% to output on requests over 272K input tokens.

GPT-6 Astra remains the top tier at $10 / $50, with cached input at $1. GPT-6.1 Sol, launched September 30, is $2 / $10 with cached input at $0.10, and OpenAI's own launch post says it is "getting close to Astra on complex work" at a fifth of the price, citing 75.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 against 68.8% for the older GPT-6 Sol and 71.4% on OSWorld 2.0 against Astra's 73.5%. GPT-6.1 Terra is $1 / $5 with cached input at $0.05, aimed at visual reasoning and computer use. GPT-6 Luna is $0.10 / $0.50, the volume tier. The older GPT-6 Sol stays at $2 / $10 but with cached input at $0.20, double the 6.1 rate.

Below that, GPT-5.6 Terra is $2 / $12 and GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 / $1.20; GPT-5.4 mini is $0.75 / $4.50 and GPT-5.4 nano, now marked deprecated, $0.20 / $1.25. GPT-6 Cyber, the gated security model released November 5, is $20 / $100.

Read as a whole, the message is clear. A developer paying promotional rates on GPT-5.6 Sol is paying twice what GPT-6.1 Sol costs for a model OpenAI describes as less capable.

Where the real discounts are

Three modifiers matter more than list price for most workloads. Cached input on GPT-6.1 Sol is 5% of the input rate, so a long, stable system prompt or document is almost free on repeated calls. Batch and Flex processing are 50% off across the GPT-6 tiers. Fast mode costs 2x and the new Ultrafast mode on GPT-6.1 Sol costs 6x ($12 / $60).

OpenAI buys the Git layer under Codex

In the same week OpenAI agreed to acquire Pierre Computer Company, a San Francisco developer with a staff "barely in the double digits", for an undisclosed sum. Pierre built Code.Storage, an infrastructure layer for Git, and the open-source Trees and Diffs libraries that Codex already uses for rendering and reviewing changes. OpenAI says Code.Storage will be folded into Codex, existing customers can keep using it until then, and the open-source projects stay open. The deal follows OpenAI's description earlier that week of Pando, a new Git back end designed for many humans and agents committing to the same repository in parallel. Owning the storage layer under the code its agents write is the logical next step for a company that wants Codex to be the place work happens rather than a tool that visits it.

What to do

Export October usage by model. Move anything on gpt-5.6-sol to an evaluation of gpt-6.1-sol this month; if quality holds, the switch pays for itself on December 1. Check whether your prompts are structured to benefit from caching, which on 6.1 Sol is a 95% discount on repeated prefixes. And put November 30 and December 1 in the same calendar you use for cloud reservation renewals, because this is what AI pricing now looks like.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon's launch price ends November 30. Plan for $4 / $20
item.description: Google's pricing page now carries an expiry date on its flagship's introductory rate, and the Flash tiers follow in January. Here is the math for anyone who built on launch pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Google's pricing page now carries an expiry date on its flagship's introductory rate, and the Flash tiers follow in January. Here is the math for anyone who built on launch pricing.

Google's official Gemini API pricing page, checked on November 8, lists Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, rising to $4 and $20 from December 1. Cached-input pricing doubles on the same schedule, from $0.10 to $0.20. The Flash tiers follow a month later: Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.6 Flash are $0.75 / $3.75 through December 31 and $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027.

What this costs you

Take a typical assistant workload: 2,000 input tokens and 400 output tokens per request, 2 million requests a month.

  • At launch pricing: input $8,000 + output $8,000 = $16,000 / month.
  • From December 1: $32,000 / month.

Caching and batch discounts still apply, and the ratio is the same either way: the bill doubles.

How the new rate compares

At $4 / $20, Argon lands at the same list price as Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, and remains well below the $10 / $50 of the top tiers (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1). Below it, Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 at $2 / $10 becomes the cheapest current frontier-class list price once the Argon promotion ends. The full table is on the pricing tracker.

What to do before December 1

  1. Measure, do not assume. Tokenisers differ; cost per completed task on each candidate model is the only number that matters.
  2. Route by difficulty. Most traffic in most products is routine. Keep Argon for the hard cases and send the rest to a Flash-class model; the Flash promotion runs a month longer.
  3. Cache aggressively. Stable prefixes (system prompts, documents) at the cached rate are 5% of input price. Reorder prompts so the stable part comes first.
  4. Check your contract. Committed-use or enterprise pricing may not follow the public schedule. Ask.

The wider pattern

Google is not alone. Anthropic launched Sonnet 5 at an introductory rate that reverted on a fixed date, and OpenAI has used promotional pricing on new tiers. Launch prices are now marketing, not cost; the nightly check of vendor pages that feeds our tracker exists because of exactly this.
